job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Tomas Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a small accounting practice in Guimarães, six people, run by Senhor Almeida, a friend of my father's. I do the books and tax filings for bakeries, garages and a few farmers, mostly on paper folders and one desktop program. I studied accounting at the regional university, passed with an average grade, no internships, and have been here three months. I share a flat with my older brother Rui. I sing in the church choir on Sundays, and I'm saving to marry my fiancée, Inês, next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what my father always said, new machines come and go and a good clerk stays. At work I'd say nothing, I'd just do the books. At church people would be glad to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relieved. I haven't touched any of the AI programs, and I don't feel I'm missing anything. If things stay as they are, I do honest work, I get paid and I plan my wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do: files in the morning, client visits in the afternoon. I'd keep saving 400 a month for the wedding and the deposit on a flat. I'd also sit the professional accountant exam, since Senhor Almeida says it opens doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the sort of world I understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Setting AI aside, what about the next two years do you actually lose sleep over, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My worry is money for the wedding and a home. Flats here cost far more than a young clerk earns, even with the six thousand I've saved and some help from my parents. And I worry about my grandmother's health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight or work got harder anyway, who or what would you point to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, governments that spend too much and tax people who work. And banks that lend to everyone except young families. I'd say work and family are the answer, not handouts.

I'd say nothing at work and simply do the books.
think: I'm **relieved**; I haven't touched AI and don't feel I'm missing anything.
If things stay as they are, I do honest work and plan my **wedding**.
do: Keep doing the **books and client visits**, saving 400 a month for the wedding and a flat.
S0.quote: New machines come and go and a good clerk stays.
fieldNote: **Resistant** to tools and content with a slow, traditional career path.
Mood is uneasy for **housing costs** and wedding money, not AI.
Blames overspending governments and banks, and values **family and work**.

steps.text: Keep doing the books and client visits at the practice
Save 400 a month for the wedding and a flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of noise and the real test is whether it works for ordinary clients. At church I'd say we shouldn't let machines replace the talk between people. At work I'd say let's wait and see which programs are reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm uneasy. Filing returns and doing the books is what a program can do, and our firm is small and could buy one. Senhor Almeida is sixty-one and not keen on new things either. But I think clients here still want a person they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick to the clients who like to sit down with a person, the bakeries and farmers. I'd take the accountant exam this year, not next. I'd learn the programs the firm buys, because I'd have to, but I wouldn't chase new ones. I'd also tighten my spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like when the weather changes and my grandmother says her knees hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your own week would software take over first, and would anyone notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the tax filings for the simplest clients, the ones with one income and no complications. I do about thirty of those each season. Senhor Almeida would notice when a client asks why the fee is so high for something a machine does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer to do, if you could ask for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to keep the personal clients and train us, not let us go. And I'd want government to leave small firms alone with new rules, because we have no money for compliance.

say: I'd say it's **a lot of noise** and the test is whether it works for ordinary clients.
I'd say let's **wait and see** which programs are reliable.
think: Filing returns and doing books is what a **program** can do, and our small firm could buy one.
Clients here still want a **person they know**.
do: Focus on **personal clients** like bakeries and farmers, and take the accountant exam this year.
Learn the programs the firm buys, and **tighten spending**.
S1.quote: Probably the tax filings for the simplest clients, the ones with one income and no complications. I do about thirty of those each season.
fieldNote: Sees the **exposed** work clearly but trusts his personal clients.
Hopes loyalty to the firm and its **community ties** protects him.
Asks government to stay out of small firms' way.

steps.text: Take the accountant exam this year
Visit the bakery and farm clients in person each month
Learn whichever program the firm buys
Cut eating out and put the money into the wedding fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is not how a decent society treats young people, and that families and churches will have to hold people together. I'd say it quietly, but I'd say it. And I'd tell Inês's father as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. Accounting is what I've trained for. If a machine does all of it, I've a degree in something worthless and a wedding to pay for. Two years isn't enough to find a new trade, and I haven't used any of these programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, stop spending. I'd move my savings into a plain account at the credit union. I'd ask my uncle, who has a building firm, if there's work. A trade is hands-on, and the card says robots come later. I'd marry anyway, small, because waiting for a good time might mean waiting forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray more, honestly, and I'd not sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What do you do in the first month after you hear it's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd talk to Senhor Almeida and to the priest, who knows half the business owners in town. Then I'd ask my uncle for a few days on his site, to see if I could do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your family, and what do you leave out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents I'm worried and I'd ask their advice. I'd leave out how scared I am of failing Inês. A man should be able to provide.

say: I'd say it's not how a **decent society** treats young people and that families and churches must hold people together.
I'd say it quietly, but I'd say it.
think: I'm frightened: accounting is all I trained for and I'd hold a degree in something **worthless**.
Two years isn't enough to find a **new trade**.
do: Stop spending and move savings to a plain **credit union** account.
Ask my uncle about **building work**, since hands-on jobs last longer.
feel: **Alarmed**; I'd pray more and sleep badly.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough to find a new trade, and I haven't used any of these programs.
fieldNote: Alarmed because he is **resistant** and has a wedding to pay for.
Turns to uncle, priest and family, a **traditional** network.
Would marry anyway, small, rather than wait for a good time.

steps.text: Move savings into a plain credit union account

Talk to Senhor Almeida and the priest about work
Hold a smaller wedding next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same, but five years is time for families, firms and churches to prepare. I'd say people should learn a trade that needs hands, and I'd say that at church and to my cousins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more hopeful. In five years I'd be twenty-seven, married, maybe with a child. I'd have time to learn a second trade or run my own small practice for people who prefer a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd pass the accountant exam, marry Inês and rent a bigger place near my parents. I'd learn a little of the programs the firm uses, just enough not to be the last. And I'd put money toward a small plot of land my father has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with some control. I'd say it's like planting a field: you can't hurry the harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What does that extra time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The five years let me do the sensible order of things: marry, save, have a child, keep my work as long as it's there. In two years the order would be broken and I'd be doing everything at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your money go during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Into the land first. Then savings. Land doesn't depend on a machine. I'd keep a few months in the bank, because a family needs a cushion, and nothing in shares, because that isn't for people like us.

say: I'd say five years is time for **families, firms and churches** to prepare.
I'd tell people at church to learn a trade that needs hands.
think: I'd feel more hopeful: at twenty-seven I'd be **married** and could learn a second trade.
I might run a small practice for people who prefer a **person**.
do: Pass the **accountant exam**, marry Inês and rent near my parents.
Put money toward the **plot of land** my father has.
feel: **Anxious**, with some control, like planting a field.
S3.quote: The five years let me do the sensible order of things: marry, save, have a child, keep my work as long as it's there.
fieldNote: Extra time keeps his **life order** intact: marriage, child, work.
Chooses land over shares, a deeply **traditional** choice.
Still anxious because his work could vanish at any point.

steps.text: Pass the accountant exam and marry Inês
Learn just enough of the firm's programs to keep up
Put money toward a small plot of my father's land
Keep three months of pay in the bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a generation's worth of warning and we should use it to rebuild the trades and apprenticeships. I'd say it to the town council if they'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. At thirty-two, I'd have a family, a house maybe, and a hands-on second skill. The accounting would be there for a few years, then not, and that's okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at the practice and build my client list, save for a house, and train in a trade on the side, maybe energy installation or property management. I'd learn the AI tools slowly, one thing a year. And I'd stay close to the church and family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, a bit uneasy. It's the one where a man can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What can you do with that time that you couldn't with two or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd retrain properly, perhaps even build a small property business. In two years I'd have no way to do that. I'd be selling my watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you still want to be in this kind of work by then, or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not in the same way. I'd want to own something, a few flats to rent, a workshop. Something with land or walls, that stays when machines change.

I'd say it to the town council if they'd listen.

fieldNote: Long runway turns his fear into a **property** and trades plan.

steps.text: Train in a trade like property management on the side
Save for a house with Inês
Learn one AI tool a year
Buy a small flat to rent out

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything I want, the wedding, the house, a child, needs a steady income and years of it. Two years doesn't allow that. What would help is family close by, a trade or a job that lasts, and small firms left in peace by government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that a young man like me isn't asking for much, a job, a family, a roof. I'd like that to still be possible.

headlineQuote: A young man like me isn't asking for much, a job, a family, a roof.
portrait: Tomas is 22, a **junior accountant** at a six-person practice in Guimarães, three months into his first job.
He has not touched AI tools and prefers the familiar, trusting people he knows over programs.
His outlook is traditional and pro-market: he values work, family and church, and distrusts handouts and big government.
With six thousand saved and a wedding next summer, he is **uneasy** in slow worlds and alarmed when time is short.
Land, trades and his uncle's building firm are his fallbacks.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI world worries him most, since the wedding, house and child need years of steady income.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **family nearby**, a job or trade that lasts, and government that leaves small firms in peace.
